subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Two goods with a positive cross elasticity of demand (XED) are:
questions.explain: A positive XED means a rise in one good's price raises demand for the other, indicating substitutes.

questions.q: The Coase theorem suggests that externalities can be resolved efficiently if:
options: Property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low
The government always intervenes with taxes
questions.explain: Coase argued that with well-defined property rights and negligible bargaining costs, private parties can negotiate an efficient outcome without government.

questions.q: Price elasticity of supply (PES) tends to be more elastic when:
options: Stocks of finished goods are high and capacity is spare
The time period considered is very short
questions.explain: Spare capacity and available stocks let firms expand output quickly in response to price, raising PES.

questions.q: The free-rider problem causes public goods to be:
options: Under-provided or not provided at all by private markets
questions.explain: Because consumers can benefit without paying, firms cannot generate sufficient revenue, so the private market under-provides or fails to provide the good.

questions.q: A key advantage of tradable pollution permits over a fixed tax is that they:
options: Guarantee a precise total quantity of pollution while allowing the market to set the price
Require no government involvement at all
Always raise more revenue than a carbon tax
questions.explain: A cap-and-trade scheme fixes the aggregate quantity of emissions and lets the permit price emerge from trading, ensuring an environmental target is met.

questions.q: In the price mechanism, the rationing function refers to:
options: Prices signalling where resources should move
Prices rising to allocate scarce goods to those willing to pay
Prices incentivising producers to supply more
questions.explain: The rationing function uses rising prices to distribute scarce goods to consumers who value them most.

questions.q: Information asymmetry in a market refers to a situation where:
options: One party in a transaction has more or better information than the other
Prices fully reflect all available information
The government withholds information from firms
questions.explain: Information asymmetry occurs when one party (e.g. the seller) holds more relevant information than the other, leading to misallocation of resources.

questions.q: A pure public good is best defined as one that is:
options: Provided only by the government and free at the point of use
questions.explain: A pure public good is simultaneously non-rival (one person's use does not diminish another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be prevented from consuming it).

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand (YED) for an inferior good is:
questions.explain: An inferior good has a negative YED because demand falls as consumer income rises.

questions.q: The price elasticity of demand (PED) is calculated as:
options: % change in quantity demanded / % change in income
% change in quantity demanded / % change in price
% change in price / % change in quantity demanded
Change in quantity / change in price
questions.explain: PED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, so quantity is divided by price.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers of a good with positive externalities shifts the:
options: Supply curve to the right, lowering price and increasing output toward the social optimum
Supply curve to the left, raising price
questions.explain: A producer subsidy lowers costs, shifting supply right so output rises toward the optimum where MSB equals MSC.

questions.q: A good with a PED of -0.4 is described as:
questions.explain: A coefficient between 0 and -1 means demand is price inelastic, so quantity changes proportionately less than price.

questions.q: Which point on an externality diagram shows the socially optimal level of output?
questions.explain: Allocative efficiency is achieved where marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit, the social optimum.

questions.q: If a firm raises price and total revenue rises, demand for the product must be:
questions.explain: When demand is inelastic, the proportionate fall in quantity is smaller than the price rise, so revenue increases.

questions.q: Which is a likely unintended consequence of a high tax on sugary drinks?
options: A complete end to all consumption
A guaranteed rise in producer profits
Substitution toward untaxed but equally unhealthy products, or smuggling
questions.explain: High indirect taxes can prompt substitution to untaxed alternatives or illicit markets, an unintended consequence reducing effectiveness.

questions.q: A merit good is one that is:
options: Under-consumed because consumers underestimate its private benefit and it has positive externalities
Always provided by the free market efficiently
Over-consumed because consumers overestimate its private benefit
questions.explain: Merit goods are under-consumed because individuals undervalue the private benefit and external benefits are ignored, justifying intervention.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The total cost of all alternatives forgone
The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
The money price paid for a good
The sunk cost of a previous decision
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next best alternative sacrificed, not the sum of all alternatives.

questions.q: A positive consumption externality means that, at the free-market equilibrium, society:
options: Under-consumes the good relative to the social optimum
questions.explain: When MSB exceeds MPB, the market under-consumes because consumers ignore the external benefits, justifying a subsidy.

questions.q: An outward shift of the entire PPF is most likely caused by:
options: An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production
A movement from inside to a point on the curve
A reallocation of resources between the two goods
questions.explain: Economic growth shifting the PPF outward requires more or better resources or improved technology.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers will, ceteris paribus:
options: Shift the supply curve to the right and lower equilibrium price
Shift the demand curve to the right
Shift the supply curve to the left and raise price
questions.explain: A subsidy lowers production costs, shifting supply right, increasing quantity and lowering market price.

questions.q: Compared with regulation, an advantage of a market-based solution such as a tax is that it:
options: Provides a continuous incentive to reduce the harmful activity and raises revenue
Sets an exact legal limit on the activity
Cannot be passed on to consumers
Removes the need for any monitoring
questions.explain: A tax gives firms an ongoing financial incentive to cut the externality at every unit and generates revenue, unlike a fixed legal limit.

questions.q: A 'nudge' in behavioural economics is a policy that:
options: Imposes a large tax to change behaviour
Alters the choice architecture to influence behaviour without removing options
questions.explain: Nudges change the way choices are presented to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice.

questions.q: If supply is perfectly elastic, the supply curve is:
questions.explain: Perfectly elastic supply is horizontal because firms supply any quantity at a single given price.

questions.q: A maximum price (price ceiling) set below the equilibrium will cause:
questions.explain: A binding price ceiling holds price below equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.

questions.q: In behavioural economics, 'bounded rationality' refers to the idea that:
options: Decision-making is limited by information, time and cognitive capacity
questions.explain: Bounded rationality recognises that limited information and mental capacity prevent fully rational optimisation.

questions.q: Government failure occurs when intervention:
options: Increases consumer surplus without any cost
Results in a net welfare loss or a misallocation of resources
questions.explain: Government failure arises when state intervention causes a more inefficient allocation of resources than would have existed otherwise.

questions.q: Moral hazard arises when:
options: A party changes its behaviour after a transaction because it no longer bears full risk
Buyers and sellers have identical information
questions.explain: Moral hazard occurs post-contract when one party takes greater risks because the costs fall on another party, a result of asymmetric information.

questions.q: A behavioural 'nudge' is a form of intervention that:
options: Alters the choice architecture to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice
questions.explain: Nudges change the way choices are presented (e.g. default options) to influence decisions without removing options or using price.

questions.q: At the midpoint of a straight-line, downward-sloping demand curve, PED is:
questions.explain: Along a straight-line demand curve, the midpoint has unit elasticity where total revenue is maximised.

questions.q: Making automatic pension enrolment the default option exploits which behavioural insight?
questions.explain: Default options exploit inertia, as people tend to stick with the pre-set choice rather than opt out.
